reference.source: Firestein & Kelley's Textbook of Rheumatology / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: A benign, self-limiting cause of cervical lymphadenopathy, classically in young women of Asian descent
Presents with tender posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, fever, and sometimes night sweats, weight loss, and a maculopapular rash
Leucopenia with atypical lymphocytes is a common laboratory clue
The main clinical importance is that it mimics lymphoma and tuberculous lymphadenitis, and it can be confused with lupus lymphadenopathy on histology
Diagnosis rests on excisional lymph node biopsy showing paracortical necrosis with abundant histiocytes and karyorrhectic debris and a characteristic absence of neutrophils
There is a recognised association with systemic lupus erythematosus, which may precede, coincide with, or follow the lymphadenitis
Management is supportive with analgesia and antipyretics; corticosteroids are reserved for severe or recurrent disease
reference.pathophysiology: Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease is a self-limiting histiocytic necrotising lymphadenitis of uncertain cause, thought to represent an exuberant T-cell and histiocyte-mediated immune response, possibly triggered by a viral or other infectious agent in a genetically predisposed individual. Affected lymph nodes show paracortical zones of coagulative necrosis populated by proliferating histiocytes, plasmacytoid dendritic cells, and CD8-positive T lymphocytes, with prominent karyorrhectic (apoptotic) debris and a striking paucity of neutrophils and plasma cells. The same mechanisms of immune dysregulation link it to systemic lupus erythematosus.
additionalDifferentials: Reactive or viral lymphadenitis (including infectious mononucleosis)
additionalInvestigations: Excisional lymph node biopsy showing paracortical necrosis, karyorrhexis, and histiocytes without neutrophils
Full blood count and film often showing leucopenia with atypical lymphocytes
Inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP) and lactate dehydrogenase
Autoimmune screen including antinuclear antibody to assess for associated lupus
Investigations to exclude tuberculosis and other infective causes
Cross-sectional imaging if lymphoma is a concern
redFlags: Persistent or progressive lymphadenopathy raising concern for lymphoma
Development of features of systemic lupus erythematosus
Prolonged high fever or systemic deterioration
Rare aseptic meningitis or other extranodal involvement
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and usually resolves spontaneously over several weeks to a few months; recurrence occurs in a minority, and patients warrant follow-up for the possible later emergence of systemic lupus erythematosus.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing it as lymphoma on histology and initiating unnecessary treatment
Failing to consider or later screen for systemic lupus erythematosus
Relying on fine-needle aspiration, which is often non-diagnostic, rather than excisional biopsy
Mistaking the necrosis for tuberculous lymphadenitis
Prescribing antibiotics for a non-infective, self-limiting condition
management: Reassurance and observation, since the necrotising lymphadenitis is benign and self-limiting, resolving over weeks to months
Symptomatic relief with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and antipyretics for fever and tender lymphadenopathy
A course of corticosteroids for severe, persistent or systemic disease, with hydroxychloroquine considered for refractory or recurrent cases
Confirm the diagnosis on excisional biopsy and exclude the key mimics, lymphoma and tuberculous lymphadenitis, before settling on conservative care
Screen for and monitor associated systemic lupus erythematosus with antinuclear antibody and clinical review, as it may precede, coincide with or follow the lymphadenitis
Rheumatology or haematology referral where diagnosis is uncertain or the course is atypical
Structured follow-up for recurrence and for later emergence of lupus
